title: Does Your Team Have Vision Fatigue?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article names a condition it calls Vision Fatigue, in which a team that has seen little progress over a long period responds with irritation to renewed talk of the big picture. Repeating the vision through successive setbacks does not motivate people; it annoys them and can prompt them to mock the vision. The author admits there is no clear marker, but suggests that a few months of slowdown is not enough while six months to a year of poor performance is. His prescription is to shift from aspirational speeches to new tactics and concrete action. The closing image contrasts looking skyward for inspiration with grabbing a ladder to climb out.
points: Vision Fatigue sets in when a long stretch without progress makes repeated vision talk irritating rather than motivating.
Symptoms include mocking the vision, craving short-term milestones, and negativity toward anything big picture.
A rough threshold is given: a few months of slowdown is normal, but six months to a year of poor performance signals the problem.
The remedy is new tactics and actions, not a rehash of long-range aspirations.
quotes: For leaders, keeping the vision and long-range goals front and center for the team is essential work. Team members are more engaged and confident when they know where the ship is headed and how the organization plans to get there. But when progress is slow or inhibited over a long period of time
Leaders who frequently articulate the vision in the face of successive setbacks or inertia don’t motivate anyone. They irritate people, instead.

Once a team has vision fatigue, they respond negatively to anything big picture. They crave new tactics and the celebration of short-term milestones, but find the optimism and confidence leaders have in the vision to be overblown and annoying. It’s not uncommon for team members with Vision Fatigue to make fun of the vision or to decry its articulation at yet another team meeting.

Unfortunately, there is no line in the sand or critical marker that tells a leader that the team is experiencing Vision Fatigue. The best call is to presume that any successive failure or lack of progress may suggest the need for new tactics and actions rather than a rehash of the long-range goals and vision.

At that point, team members look to leaders for answers and a way out of the doldrums, not an impassioned speech about the organization’s aspirations and dreams. If leadership is the capacity to translate a vision into a reality, then sometimes the focus on reality takes precedence.

Leaders need to be reminded that digging the team out of a deep hole doesn’t require everyone to look toward the sky for inspiration. Rather, it demands everyone grab a ladder and begin the climb out.
